01 / The story

The mission.
The journey.
The record.

From Honolulu, Hawaii, to the New York City finish, William Goodge covered a marathon-distance course in every U.S. state. The route compressed fifty starts, recovery windows, and constant travel into a single continuous operation.

The numbers tell one part of the story. The lasting account is about the athlete, the crew, the people who joined along the way, and the reason William kept moving.

Mission America recorded a 22-day, 17-hour, 16-minute and 34-second completion across all 50 U.S. states. The final event time is shown as recorded by Mission America; no independent certification badge is displayed.

Watch the full story →

02 / William Goodge

The person
inside the miles.

William began running after losing his mother, Amanda, to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma in 2018. The miles became a way to carry her memory and support people affected by cancer.

Before Mission America, he ran 2,361 miles across Australia in just over 35 days and 3,011 miles from Los Angeles to New York in 55 days. Every project has been both a fundraiser and a tribute.

03 / Made possible by Goodwin

Impossible is just
a logistics problem.

An athlete can run 1,310 miles. Getting him to fifty starting lines—from Hawaii and Alaska through the mainland, then into New York—was a different endurance event entirely.

Goodwin coordinated private aviation, commercial airlines, RV transfers, route sequencing, timing, recovery windows, and real-time operational intelligence to keep the mission moving.

The legacy

The first chapter
is complete.

Mission America opened the Goodwin Endurance Series: ambitious human challenges made possible by exacting technology, logistics, and the people prepared to solve what comes next.

The idea grew from Goodwin’s founder running with William and recognizing that airplanes could become “time machines”—turning an audacious endurance plan into a coordinated national mission.

For Amanda—and for everyone affected by cancer.
